decisions.final: *(Formula reference: the finalised December 2017 standard sets $\text{ILM} = \ln\left[\exp(1) - 1 + \left(\tfrac{LC}{BIC}\right)^{0.8}\right]$, with $LC = 15 \times$ average annual operational risk losses over the previous ten years. The plain-ratio form without the 0.8 exponent comes from the March 2016 consultative document. No question in this set requires the ILM to be computed.)*
decisions.reason: Source front matter has the history reversed. The finalised Dec 2017 standard (BCBS d424, OPE25) uses ILM = ln(e - 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8) with LC = 15 x average annual losses over 10 years; the plain ratio is the March 2016 SMA consultative form. Curriculum notes for Ch 24 (12_OR_ORR24.tex L74) also carry the ^0.8 exponent. Numerically the two forms differ (LC/BIC=1.1236: 1.0445 vs 1.0353). The JSON note instructs candidates to use the wrong formula, so it must be replaced; key (a) unaffected. Replace only the final parenthetical paragraph. Out-of-slice follow-up: other OR.json items that print the plain-ratio ILM should be checked.

decisions.final: In the cloud provider breach (Capital One on AWS), a former employee of the cloud provider exploited a misconfigured firewall to reach unencrypted customer data. Both firms knew of the vulnerability, and the bank was still held ultimately responsible and fined USD 80 million for inadequate risk management of its cloud provider.
decisions.reason: Source (PDF p.13) says 'contractor at the provider exploiting the provider's own misconfigured firewall'. Curriculum notes (19_OR_ORR13.tex) say a former AWS employee exploited a weakness in the cloud storage firewall, both Capital One and AWS knew of the vulnerability, data was unencrypted, and Capital One was fined USD 80m for inadequate vendor risk management. 'Contractor' is wrong; 'provider's own firewall' misstates the facts (the misconfigured WAF was Capital One's). Proposed sentence matches the curriculum. Key (a) unaffected.

decisions.final: The clearest large-scale illustration sits in Chapter 1 of the curriculum rather than among this chapter's case studies: the payment protection insurance episode, where the Lloyds Banking Group paid GBP 21.9 billion, roughly USD 28 billion, in regulatory fines and customer compensation over 2015 to 2019 for failing to handle claims fairly and for misinforming customers when selling insurance alongside banking products. The Chapter 14 case studies themselves are UBS (2008, selling risky securities as safe, by far the largest penalty of the three), JPMorgan (2020, USD 920 million for spoofing, a market-manipulation case) and Deutsche Bank (2022, USD 2 million for failing to obtain best execution for client trades). Their lesson is that misrepresentation to clients draws the heaviest sanctions, while even technical breaches such as order execution are penalised.
decisions.reason: Problem is real: the Ch 14 notes (35_OR_ORR14.tex LO 53b) list UBS 2008, JPMorgan 2020 spoofing (USD 920m) and Deutsche Bank 2022 best execution (USD 2m); Lloyds PPI is not a Ch 14 case. But the auditor's fix is partly wrong: the Lloyds PPI example IS in the curriculum (Ch 1 fines table, used by OR-T2-28 and OR-T4-08, which explicitly say it 'sits outside this chapter'), and the curriculum itself dates it '2015 to 2019', so that period should be kept, not dropped. Fix: keep the PPI example attributed to Ch 1 and add the actual Ch 14 cases. Replace only the flagged sentence. Key (a) still the best of the four options.
